340:
An adjuration is a deeply solemn, serious appeal or command — one that carries extraordinary urgency and moral weight. It is not a casual request, not a polite ask, and not an ordinary order. It sits somewhere between a heartfelt plea and a binding command, charged with gravity and sincerity.

The single thing that makes an adjuration distinct from every other kind of appeal is this: it invokes something sacred, holy, or supremely important to give the request or command its binding force. The person making the adjuration essentially says, "I am asking you in the name of something you cannot ignore — God, truth, your soul, your oath."

The word adjuration is used in two closely related but distinguishable ways:

1. A solemn, earnest entreaty made by invoking a higher power

This is the most common use. When someone makes an adjuration in this sense, they are pressing another person with the deepest possible urgency — not just asking, but almost binding them morally by calling upon something sacred. The force of the appeal comes from what is invoked: God, a holy name, a sacred oath, conscience, or something the listener holds dear.

Think of it this way: if ordinary asking is a knock on a door, an adjuration is falling to one's knees at that door and saying, "I beg you in the name of God — you must answer me." There is desperation in it, but also authority.

2. A formal ritual command used to compel spiritual or supernatural forces

This is the older, more religious or ceremonial use. In religious rites, an adjuration is a set formula — a solemn charge — spoken to compel a spirit, a demon, or a divine force to act, stop, reveal, or depart. Exorcism prayers, for instance, are filled with adjurations. The speaker is not requesting the spirit to leave; they are commanding it, but doing so in the name of God or a holy authority that gives the command its power. Without invoking that authority, the command would carry no force.
What Makes It Feel Different from Similar Words

It helps to compare adjuration to nearby words:

  • A request is polite and optional. You can decline it.
  • A command has authority but doesn't necessarily carry spiritual or emotional gravity.
  • A plea is emotional and urgent but lacks the formal, invoking element.
  • An oath is a promise you make about your own behavior.
  • An adjuration combines the urgency of a plea, the seriousness of a command, and the binding weight of an oath — but it is directed outward at someone else, and it draws its power from invoking something greater than the speaker themselves.

The invoking element is the heart of it. Without that element — without the sense that something sacred or supremely binding is being called upon — it would just be a very strong request. With it, it becomes an adjuration.

Adjuration is a formal, elevated word. You will not hear it in everyday conversation. You will encounter it most often in:

  • Religious texts and scripture (it appears repeatedly in the Bible, for example, where priests, prophets, or individuals put someone under solemn oath by invoking God)
  • Historical literature and formal writing
  • Legal or ceremonial language where oaths and formal charges appear
  • Serious literary fiction where a character implores another with the utmost gravity

When you see the word, it signals that what is being described is not light or casual — it is a moment of maximum seriousness.
Concrete Examples to Fix the Meaning

Example 1 — The religious/ritual sense:
In the Gospel of Matthew, the high priest says to Jesus during his trial: "I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ." This is a classic adjuration. He is not simply asking. He is formally charging Jesus, in the name of God, to answer — invoking divine authority to make the demand binding and unavoidable.

Example 2 — The earnest entreaty sense:
A father on his deathbed, gripping his son's hand and saying, "I adjure you — swear to me before God that you will look after your mother and your brothers" — that is an adjuration. The dying man is pressing his son with every ounce of moral weight available to him, invoking God to make the appeal as binding as possible.

Example 3 — A slightly more literary use:
A character in a novel might write in a letter: "I send you this as my adjuration — by everything we once shared, by every promise you ever made me, do not let them destroy what we built." Even without naming God explicitly, the writer is invoking the sacred weight of shared memory and past promises to give their appeal its gravity.

An adjuration is a solemn, urgent appeal or command that draws its binding force from invoking something sacred, holy, or supremely authoritative — making it far more than an ordinary request and closer to a moral charge that the recipient cannot easily dismiss.
341: To adjure someone means to urgently and solemnly urge, appeal to, or command them to do — or not do — something. It is never a light or casual request. It always carries a sense of gravity, seriousness, and high stakes.

Imagine a moment where the stakes are extremely high — a deathbed scene, a courtroom, a last desperate conversation between two people. In those moments, saying "please" or "I'm asking you to" doesn't feel weighty enough. The speaker reaches for something stronger, something that binds the other person more deeply. That is when someone adjures.

When you adjure someone, you are not simply asking. You are making an appeal with everything you have — your authority, your moral weight, your desperation, or the sacredness of something like a vow, a name, or a bond. The word suggests that the speaker wants to make it as hard as possible for the other person to refuse — not through force, but through the sheer seriousness of the appeal.

Adjure carries two shades of meaning that often blend into each other:

1. To solemnly and earnestly beg or urge
This is a heartfelt, solemn plea. The speaker is appealing with deep seriousness.

"She adjured him not to throw his life away on this foolish decision."

2. To formally command or charge someone
This is more authoritative. The speaker has a position of power and is formally binding someone to an action.

"The judge adjured the witness to tell the whole truth."

In both senses, the key quality is identical: this is not an everyday request. It is earnest, weighty, and loaded with consequence.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is important because adjure has several close relatives, but none of them are quite the same:

  • Ask / request — purely neutral, no solemnity whatsoever.
  • Beg — shows raw desperation and emotion, but lacks the formal or sacred dimension.
  • Urge — suggests encouragement, but is too mild and lacks gravity.
  • Implore / entreat — these come closest. They are emotional, earnest appeals. But adjure adds an extra layer: it often invokes something sacred, authoritative, or binding — an oath, a name, a moral duty, a relationship — to reinforce the appeal.
  • Command / order — purely authoritative with no emotional or sacred weight. Adjure is different because it appeals to the other person's conscience, sense of honour, or feeling of obligation, rather than just issuing a directive.

The unique flavour of adjure is this combination: the urgency of pleading + the weight of authority or sanctity. It sits somewhere between a plea and a command.

One very common and important grammatical pattern with adjure is: adjure someone by something. This means the speaker is making the appeal in the name of — or anchored to — something the other person holds sacred or dear: God, an oath, a shared history, a deep bond.

"He adjured her by their years of friendship to reconsider."
"The priest adjured the congregation by the name of God to examine their hearts."

This "by something" pattern is one of the features that makes adjure distinctly itself. The appeal isn't floating in the air — it is grounded in something that gives it moral or sacred force.

Adjure always takes a person as its object — you adjure someone. After that, you typically use the infinitive form (to + verb) to say what you want them to do.

The full pattern looks like this:
adjure + [person] + (by something) + to do something

"I adjure you to keep this secret."
"He adjured her by all that was holy to stay."

Adjure is a formal word. You would never hear it in everyday small talk ("I adjure you to pass the salt"). It appears most naturally in:

  • Literary or religious writing — where the language is elevated and the stakes are high.
  • Legal or official settings — a judge formally adjuring a witness; a solemn oath being administered.
  • High-stakes dramatic moments in fiction — characters making desperate, binding appeals to each other.
  • Formal speeches or moral declarations — a leader adjuring a nation to rise to its responsibilities.

• "The dying queen adjured her successor to protect the people above all else."
  • "I adjure you, by everything we have shared, not to go down this path."
  • "The general adjured his soldiers to hold the line, whatever the cost."
  • "The prophet adjured the people to turn away from wrongdoing before it was too late."
  • "She adjured the court, in the name of justice, to consider the evidence carefully."

To adjure is to make a solemn, urgent, and deeply serious appeal to someone — urging or commanding them to do or refrain from doing something. It carries moral weight, often invokes something sacred or authoritative, and lives somewhere between a heartfelt plea and a formal command. It is the word you reach for when an ordinary request simply does not feel strong enough for what the moment demands.
342:
To adjust means to make a small, careful change to something so that it becomes more correct, more comfortable, or more suitable for a purpose.

Think of it this way: something is mostly fine, but not quite right. Adjusting it means you're fine-tuning it — nudging it toward the ideal state. You are not replacing it, rebuilding it, or fixing something that is broken. You are simply bringing it closer to where it needs to be.

A tailor adjusts your shirt — he takes it in a little at the sides. He isn't making a new shirt. He's making this one fit you better.
The Two Main Ways "Adjust" Is Used

1. You Adjust a Thing (You Change Something)

Here, "adjust" is about physically or practically changing an object, a setting, a plan, a number, or anything external — so that it works better or suits the situation better.

Examples:

  • She adjusted the brightness of her phone screen because the sunlight was too strong.
  • He adjusted his tie before walking into the meeting room.
  • The engineer adjusted the pressure in the machine so it wouldn't overheat.
  • The teacher adjusted the lesson plan after realizing the students needed more time.
  • Please adjust the volume — it's too loud.
  • The dentist adjusted the position of the brace.

In every case, notice: the thing existed and worked in some way, but a small, deliberate change made it more suitable.

2. You Adjust Yourself (You Adapt to Something New)

This is the second, equally important meaning. When a situation or environment is new or different, and you change your behavior, habits, feelings, or expectations to match it — you are adjusting.

This is almost always written as "adjust to" something.

Examples:

  • It took her several months to adjust to her new city.
  • Children usually adjust to a new school faster than their parents expect.
  • After his knee injury, he had to adjust to walking with a cane.
  • When I moved to a colder country, I found it hard to adjust to the weather.
  • He lost his job, and the whole family had to adjust to a tighter budget.

Here, "adjust" doesn't mean you are fixing yourself. It means you are responding to a changed reality by gradually changing how you live, think, or feel. The key idea is a process — it takes time, effort, or discomfort, and eventually things settle into a new normal.

The word "adjust" carries three quiet but important implications:

  1. The change is small or moderate, not total. If you are rebuilding something from the ground up, or making a massive transformation, "adjust" sounds wrong. You don't "adjust" a building — you renovate it. But you do adjust a single door that doesn't close properly.
  2. The change is intentional and purposeful. You're not randomly changing something — you are targeting a specific problem and correcting for it.
  3. The thing being adjusted was mostly already there. It just needed a little correction, alignment, or fine-tuning. A good analogy: if your car is running roughly, a mechanic might adjust the engine timing — not replace the engine.

Adjust vs. Fix
"Fix" implies something was broken or wrong. "Adjust" implies something was merely not perfectly suited yet.

  • You fix a broken tap. You adjust the water pressure.

Adjust vs. Change
"Change" is a broad word — it can mean anything from a tiny tweak to a complete overhaul. "Adjust" specifically means a small, targeted change.

  • You might change your entire career. But you adjust your schedule to make space for a new class.

Adjust vs. Adapt
"Adapt" and "adjust to" are very close in meaning when talking about people. But "adapt" often implies a bigger, more fundamental shift — sometimes even a change in identity or structure. "Adjust" is softer, smaller, and more everyday.

  • A species adapts over thousands of years. A person adjusts to a new routine within weeks.

Adjust vs. Tweak
"Tweak" means almost the same thing as adjust, but it is more informal and implies an even tinier change.

  • You adjust the recipe. You tweak it again after tasting it.
Common Collocations (Words That Naturally Go with "Adjust")

Knowing what words typically appear near "adjust" will help you use it naturally:

  • Adjust the settings / the temperature / the volume / the contrast
  • Adjust your expectations / your plans / your approach / your attitude
  • Adjust the mirror / the seat / the strap
  • Adjust to life / to change / to a new job / to the time zone
  • Adjust accordingly — this very common phrase means "to change in a way that responds suitably to a situation"
    • "We don't know yet how many guests are coming, but we'll adjust accordingly."

The adjective well-adjusted is commonly used to describe a person. It means someone who is emotionally healthy, stable, and capable of handling life's challenges without falling apart. Such a person has successfully managed to adjust to the realities of the world around them.

  • "Despite a difficult childhood, she grew up to be a confident and well-adjusted adult."

Its opposite, poorly adjusted, describes someone who struggles to cope or fit into their environment.

Core meaningTo make a small, careful, purposeful change so something works better or fits better
When used on things"Adjust the chair, the plan, the dosage, the settings"
When used on people"Adjust to a new place, routine, or situation" — meaning to slowly adapt
What it impliesSmall change, not total overhaul; intentional; improving fit or function

In one sentence: To adjust is to make a deliberate, small change — to a thing, a plan, or yourself — so that it better suits the situation it's in.
343: Something is "adjustable" when it can be changed, moved, set, or modified — and it was designed or intended to be that way. The central idea is the capability for controlled, deliberate change. If something is adjustable, it is not permanently locked into one fixed form. A person (or sometimes a system) can intentionally change it to better fit a need, a size, a position, or a situation.
The "-able" part matters

The ending "-able" means capable of being. So "adjustable" literally means capable of being adjusted. This is a crucial detail: it describes what something can do — its potential — not what it is doing right now.

An adjustable chair is not constantly moving up and down. It simply has the ability to be moved when you choose to move it. The capability exists and is waiting to be used.
It implies design and intention

When we call something adjustable, we almost always mean it was built or made with the ability to change — on purpose. There is a deliberate mechanism, feature, or flexibility engineered into it.

A car seat is adjustable because it has a lever or a button that slides it forward, backward, up, or down. A rubber band, by contrast, stretches — but we don't typically call it "adjustable" because it wasn't designed with deliberate, controllable settings or positions. It simply has natural elasticity. The difference is intentional design for change.
Change within limits

Adjustable does not mean unlimited or infinite change. Almost always, something adjustable can only be modified within a specific, practical range that was built into it.

An adjustable hat can fit heads of many different sizes — but it won't fit a basketball, and it won't fit a golf ball. The flexibility exists, but it exists within a defined range. This is almost always the case with adjustable things: there are boundaries to how much it can be changed.
Physical things

Many everyday objects are adjustable. A bicycle seat can be raised or lowered to suit riders of different heights. A wrench's jaw can open wider or close tighter to grip different sizes of bolts. The straps on a backpack can be lengthened or shortened for comfort. A car's side mirror can be angled to different positions for different drivers. A hospital bed can be tilted at different angles. In every case, the object was made so that a person can deliberately change its form, size, or position as needed.
Non-physical things

The word works equally well for things you cannot touch. A schedule is adjustable if meeting times can be shifted around. A loan's interest rate is adjustable if it can rise or fall over time based on market conditions. A budget is adjustable if its spending limits can be changed. A plan is adjustable if its steps can be rearranged or modified. In all these cases, the idea is identical: the thing is not permanently fixed; it can be deliberately changed to suit new circumstances.
What "adjustable" does NOT mean

It does not mean the thing is currently in the process of changing — only that it can be changed when needed. It does not mean the change happens automatically or by itself; a person or a system generally has to deliberately make the change happen. It does not mean unlimited or infinite change. And it does not mean the thing is fragile or unstable. Many adjustable things — like a heavy-duty adjustable wrench or a steel office chair — are extremely strong and sturdy. Adjustable simply means they have an intentional, controlled flexibility built into them.
Ease of use is often implied

Here is a subtlety worth knowing. In everyday language, when we call something "adjustable," we usually imply that the change is reasonably easy to make — that it was designed to be changed without a huge effort or special expertise. If something could technically be changed but requires a specialist, a factory, or enormous effort, we would not usually call it "adjustable" in conversation. The word carries a quiet suggestion of convenience and accessibility.
The opposite

The opposite of adjustable is fixed, rigid, or non-adjustable — meaning something set permanently in one position or form that cannot be changed. A fixed shelf in a bookcase always stays at the same height no matter what. An adjustable shelf can be moved up or down to different heights depending on what you need to store. "Fixed" = no change possible. "Adjustable" = change is possible and designed for.
Example sentences

"This desk is adjustable, so both tall and short people can use it comfortably."

"The doctor said the medication dosage is adjustable — it can be increased if needed."

"We need a more adjustable meeting time, since not everyone is free at 9 AM."

"The loan has an adjustable interest rate, which means the monthly payment amount can change over the years."

"The camera is mounted on an adjustable arm, so you can position it anywhere around the desk."
Comparing degrees

Like most adjectives, "adjustable" can be used in degrees of comparison. You can say something is more adjustable than another thing (it offers greater flexibility or more range of change) or the most adjustable option available. For example: "Of all the chairs in the store, this one is the most adjustable — you can change the height, the armrests, the backrest angle, and the seat tilt."
Related word forms

Adjust is the verb — it means to make a deliberate change: "Please adjust the mirror before you drive." Adjustment is the noun — it refers to the act of changing or the result of a change: "A small adjustment to the plan made everything work better." Non-adjustable is the adjective for the opposite condition: "The seat is non-adjustable, so it stays in one fixed position."
The one-line summary
If you ever need to recall the meaning in a flash: adjustable = designed to be changed in a controlled way, within limits, to fit different needs.
344: An adjutant is a military officer who serves as an administrative assistant and right-hand man to a senior commanding officer. Think of the adjutant as the person who keeps everything organized around the commander, so the commander can focus on leading and making decisions.
The Main Meaning: A Military Officer

In the military, every battalion, regiment, or brigade — basically any significant unit — has an adjutant. This person is not just a low-level helper; they are themselves an officer, but their job is to support a higher-ranking commanding officer.

What exactly does an adjutant do?

  • They handle all the administrative and organizational work of the unit — paperwork, records, correspondence, and official documentation.
  • They receive the commander's orders and communicate those orders formally to the rest of the unit. In older armies especially, the adjutant would read out orders aloud to assembled troops.
  • They coordinate between different sections, departments, or units on behalf of the commander.
  • They manage the daily functioning of the headquarters — schedules, rosters, personnel records, and similar matters.
  • In battle situations, they may relay the commander's instructions and ensure coordination happens smoothly.

Essentially, a commanding officer can't do everything alone. The adjutant is the person who makes sure all the administrative machinery runs properly, so nothing falls through the cracks. If the commander is the brain, the adjutant is often the hands that execute all the organizational tasks.

A simple way to picture it: Imagine the most senior general of an army base. He has strategy to think about, troops to command, and decisions to make. He cannot personally track every piece of paperwork, every official correspondence, every order that needs to be drafted and distributed. The adjutant does all of that. The adjutant is the officer right beside him, keeping the administrative world in order.

An adjutant is typically a relatively junior officer (in many armies, a captain or a lieutenant), but because of their direct access to the commander and their role in communications and records, they carry considerable importance and authority within the unit. When the adjutant speaks, people understand they are often speaking on behalf of the commander.

In many armies, there is also a higher position called the Adjutant General — a senior officer who handles personnel administration, records, and military manpower at an army-wide or national level. Think of this as the adjutant's role scaled up to an entire army or country.

While "adjutant" is almost always a military term, you will occasionally see it used more loosely to describe any close aide or administrative assistant to someone in a position of authority. However, this usage is rare, and when you encounter the word, it almost certainly refers to the military role.

There is a second, entirely different meaning of the word. An adjutant is also the common name for a large species of stork found in South Asia and Southeast Asia — specifically the Greater Adjutant and the Lesser Adjutant.

These birds got this name because of the way they walk: stiff, upright, and formal — almost like a soldier standing at attention or marching with rigid posture. People thought they looked like military adjutants on parade. They are large, somewhat ungainly birds, often seen near wetlands, garbage dumps, and open fields.

So if someone in a wildlife or nature context mentions an adjutant, they are talking about this bird, not a military officer.

SenseWhat it means
Military (primary)An officer who assists a senior commander with administration, communications, and organization
Bird (secondary)A large stork in South/Southeast Asia, named for its stiff, soldier-like posture

Think of the word "adjust" — an adjutant adjusts and manages everything around the commander, making sure the unit runs smoothly. The adjutant is the person who adjusts the system so that the leader can lead without being buried in details.
345:
If something is adjuvant, it means it is helping, assisting, or boosting something else — but crucially, it is not the main thing doing the work. It plays a supporting role that makes the primary thing more effective.

Think of it this way: if a superhero is the main fighter, an adjuvant is the sidekick who makes the superhero stronger, faster, or more effective. The sidekick doesn't win the battle alone — but without the sidekick, the superhero wouldn't be as powerful.
Where You'll Actually Encounter This Word

"Adjuvant" as an adjective is almost exclusively used in medicine and science. You will very rarely, if ever, see it in everyday conversation. But within medical writing and oncology (cancer care) especially, it is extremely common.

1. Adjuvant Therapy (Medicine & Cancer Treatment)

This is the most common use of the word.

When a patient has surgery to remove a tumor, doctors sometimes follow that surgery with adjuvant therapy — such as chemotherapy, radiation, or hormone therapy. Here, the word "adjuvant" tells you that:

  • The surgery was the primary treatment (the main attack).
  • The chemotherapy or radiation is the adjuvant treatment — it comes after, in a supporting role, to mop up any cancer cells that may have been left behind and to reduce the chances of the cancer returning.

So "adjuvant chemotherapy" doesn't mean the chemotherapy is unimportant. It means it is playing a helper role relative to the surgery that came first. It's assisting the overall treatment plan.

A practical way to remember it: adjuvant therapy = backup treatment that boosts the chances of success.

2. Adjuvant Effect (Immunology & Vaccines)

In vaccine science, a substance can have an adjuvant effect, meaning it boosts the immune response triggered by the vaccine.

Vaccines work by introducing something (like a piece of a virus) to teach your immune system to recognize and fight it. Sometimes, that alone isn't enough to create a strong immune response. So scientists add a substance that has an adjuvant effect — it essentially signals your immune system to pay more attention and respond more strongly, making the vaccine more effective.

Again, the adjuvant substance is not the vaccine itself. It is the helper that makes the vaccine work better.
The One Subtle But Important Nuance

"Adjuvant" does not just mean any kind of help. It specifically implies that:

  1. There is a primary agent or treatment doing the main job.
  2. The adjuvant thing is secondary by design — it exists to support and enhance that primary thing.
  3. The adjuvant element typically could not succeed on its own in the same role.

This is what separates "adjuvant" from simply saying "helpful." Something can be helpful while still being the main tool. But something adjuvant is, by definition, the secondary, enhancing force — never the primary one.
A Simple One-Sentence Definition to Anchor It All

Adjuvant describes something that assists or enhances the power of something else, where that something else is the primary force and the adjuvant element plays a deliberate, secondary supporting role.

Whenever you see the word adjuvant, ask yourself: "What is the main thing here, and what is this playing a supporting role to?" The answer to the second part of that question is what the adjuvant thing is boosting or helping. That framing will never fail you.
346: Administration refers to the act of managing, organizing, and running something — whether that something is an organization, a process, a substance, or even an estate. The word has several closely related meanings, and once you see the thread connecting them, they all make perfect sense.
1. The process of managing or running something

This is the most fundamental meaning. When people talk about the administration of a school, a hospital, a company, or a country, they mean the ongoing work of keeping it organized, making decisions, enforcing rules, and making sure everything functions smoothly.

It is not the work itself (like teaching or treating patients) — it is the management of that work.

"The administration of the university improved greatly after the new chancellor took charge."

"Running a large hospital requires careful administration."

Think of it this way: a ship needs sailors to do the actual sailing, but it also needs someone managing the route, the crew, the supplies, and the schedule. That management is the administration.
2. The group of people who do the managing

Because administration refers to the act of managing, it naturally came to also refer to the people who carry out that management. This is the collective group — the managers, officials, and support staff — responsible for running an organization.

"The administration has decided to extend the school year."

"If you have a complaint, contact the administration."

"She works in administration at the hospital."

When you walk into a college and see signs pointing to the "Administration Building," that building is where the people who manage the college — not the teachers, but the registrars, deans, HR staff, and so on — do their work.
3. A government in power (especially in American English)

In political contexts, particularly in the United States, administration refers to the government led by a sitting president, covering the entire team of officials who govern alongside them during their term in office. It also refers to the period of that government's rule.

"The Biden administration introduced new climate policies."

"This decision was made during the previous administration."

"She served in two different administrations."

This usage makes perfect sense: a president and their appointed officials are, essentially, the people administering (managing and running) the country during that period. The word packages both the people and the era into one term.

In other countries, similar bodies might be called a "government" or "cabinet," but in American English, administration is the standard word.
4. The act of giving, applying, or dispensing something

This meaning is slightly different in feel but follows the same logic. Administration can describe the formal, controlled act of delivering or applying something — usually a substance, a duty, or a formal procedure.

"The nurse was responsible for the administration of medication to patients."

"The judge oversaw the administration of the oath."

"The administration of justice must be fair and impartial."

"The administration of the exam was delayed due to a technical issue."

Here, administration implies care, authority, and a formal process. You don't just give someone a vaccine — you administer it. The noun captures that formality. It often appears in medical, legal, and official academic contexts.
5. The legal management of a deceased person's estate

In law, administration has a specific technical meaning: it is the process of managing and settling the financial affairs of someone who has died, especially when they left no will or when the executor named in the will is unable to act.

"The court granted letters of administration to her eldest son."

"The administration of the estate took over a year to complete."

A person appointed by a court to do this is called an administrator. They collect the deceased person's assets, pay off debts, and distribute what remains to rightful heirs — all under the supervision of the court. This is a formal legal process governed by specific laws.
The thread that ties all meanings together

All five meanings share the same underlying idea: organized, authoritative oversight and management of something. Whether it's running a company, governing a country, giving a patient their medicine, or settling a dead person's financial affairs — administration always involves someone (or a group) taking formal responsibility for handling a process correctly, systematically, and with authority.
Common phrases and collocations you'll encounter

• Business/public administration — a field of study focused on managing organizations or governments
  • Under the administration of — during the time something was managed by a particular person or group
  • Administration building / office — where the management staff of an institution is located
  • Trump/Obama/Biden administration — the government and its period during a U.S. president's term
  • Letters of administration — a legal document authorizing someone to manage a deceased person's estate
  • Administration of justice / law — the formal process of applying and enforcing legal principles
  • Drug/vaccine administration — the process of delivering medication to a patient
  • School/hospital administration — the managing body of those institutions

ContextWhat "administration" means

To sum it up plainly:

  • In everyday life → the management of an organization, or the people doing that management
  • In politics (especially U.S.) → the ruling government and the era of its rule
  • In medicine/law/formal settings → the act of formally giving or applying something
  • In legal inheritance → managing the estate of someone who has died

Master these five meanings and the word administration will never confuse you again — in a news article, a doctor's office, a legal document, or a conversation about politics.
347:
Almost every organized group — a company, a school, a government, a hospital — has two distinct layers of work happening at the same time.

The first layer is the main work: the actual purpose the organization exists for. Doctors treat patients. Teachers teach students. Engineers design bridges. This is the skilled, specialized work at the heart of everything.

The second layer is the management work: the organizing, coordinating, planning, and record-keeping that keeps the whole operation running smoothly behind the scenes. This second layer is what the word administrative describes.

So "administrative" means relating to the management and organization of something — whether that something is a company, a government, a school, or any institution.

Consider a hospital. The surgeons performing operations, and the nurses caring for patients — that is clinical (medical) work. But someone also has to schedule the appointments, maintain patient records, manage the budget, process insurance claims, and coordinate between departments. That is the administrative work. The people doing it hold administrative roles, and the office or department they work in is often called the administrative office or simply the administration.

The same logic applies anywhere. In a school, the teachers teach — but the principal, the registrar, and the office staff handle enrollment, timetables, school policies, and correspondence. That is the school's administrative side. In a business, the engineers or salespeople do the core work, while HR managers, office coordinators, and executive assistants handle the administrative operations.
Breaking down the most common uses

Administrative tasks or duties are the day-to-day management activities that keep an organization functioning — things like filing documents, scheduling meetings, processing paperwork, writing official correspondence, managing budgets, and maintaining records. They are not glamorous, but they are essential. Without them, even the most skilled doctors, teachers, or engineers would be lost in chaos.

Administrative staff (also called administrative personnel or admin staff) are the people whose specific job is to handle these management duties. Job titles like office manager, department coordinator, executive assistant, secretary, and registrar are all administrative roles.

An administrative decision is a decision made by those who manage or govern something, about how that thing is run or organized. For example, a university deciding to change its application process is an administrative decision. It is not a decision about academic content — it is a decision about running the institution. Similarly, a company deciding to reorganize its departments is an administrative decision.

An administrative error is a mistake that happened in the management or record-keeping process — not in the core work itself. If a hospital books two patients for the same appointment slot, that is an administrative error. If a surgeon makes a mistake during a procedure, that is a medical error. The distinction matters because it tells you where and how the mistake occurred.

Administrative procedures are the official, formal steps and processes that an organization requires people to follow in order to get things done. Filling out a form, submitting a request in writing, going through the right channels of approval — these are all parts of administrative procedure. They exist to keep things orderly, transparent, and consistent.

The word carries special weight when it comes to government, and this is worth understanding on its own.

Modern governments are typically divided into three branches: the legislative branch (which creates laws), the judicial branch (which interprets laws through courts), and the executive branch (which carries out and manages the laws in everyday life). The executive branch — made up of government departments, agencies, and offices — is fundamentally administrative in nature. It does not make the law; it administers it, meaning it puts the law into practice, enforces it, and manages the systems it creates.

This is why government bodies like a tax authority, an immigration department, an environmental protection agency, or a public health department are called administrative agencies. They administer — meaning they manage and carry out — the policies and rules that the law establishes.

Because these agencies wield significant power over people's lives (they can grant licenses, impose fines, deny permits, and make binding decisions), an entire branch of law called administrative law exists specifically to govern how they must behave. Administrative law sets the rules for what procedures agencies must follow, what powers they do and do not have, and how citizens can challenge or appeal their decisions. If a government agency makes a decision you disagree with — say, rejecting your visa application — you would typically pursue what is called an administrative appeal, which is a formal challenge within the administrative system before turning to the courts.
The feeling and tone of the word

In most everyday uses, "administrative" is a neutral, professional word. It simply describes the management and organizational side of things.

However, it sometimes takes on a slightly heavy or frustrated tone, especially in phrases like administrative burden, administrative overhead, or administrative red tape. These phrases acknowledge that management processes — while necessary — can pile up into exhausting quantities of paperwork, approval chains, and procedures that slow things down. "Administrative red tape" in particular refers to bureaucratic rules and processes that feel excessive or needlessly complicated.

On the positive side, phrases like administrative support, administrative leadership, and administrative excellence show the word being used with respect and appreciation — recognizing that good, efficient management is genuinely valuable.

"Administrative" describes anything that relates to managing, organizing, governing, or coordinating the operations of an institution, organization, or system — rather than the core, specialized work that the organization exists to perform. When something is called administrative, it belongs to the world of planning, record-keeping, decision-making about how things are run, and the formal procedures that keep organized groups functioning.
348:
"Admirable" describes someone or something that genuinely deserves respect, deep approval, and a feeling of looking up to it. When you call something admirable, you are saying it has a quality or has done something so good, so worthy, or so excellent that it naturally earns honest respect from the people who see it.

Think of it this way: when you witness something that makes you think, "Wow — that is truly worthy of respect," the thing you are looking at is admirable.
The Feeling Behind the Word

The word "admirable" is rooted in the idea of admiration — a sincere, warm feeling that combines respect with a kind of wonder. This is important because "admirable" is stronger than simply calling something "good" or "nice." You can like a meal. You can enjoy a song. But admiration — and therefore the label "admirable" — involves a deeper recognition: this thing rises above the ordinary and genuinely deserves to be looked up to.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Admirable?

Almost anything can be admirable — a person, a character trait, a decision, an action, or an achievement. But it is most naturally used for:

Moral qualities — like courage, honesty, patience, integrity, kindness, or dedication. These are the kinds of virtues that earn admiration because they are hard to maintain and represent the best of human character. "Her admirable patience never faltered, even in the most difficult moments."

Behavior in tough situations — when someone handles hardship, pressure, or challenge with grace. "He showed admirable composure during the crisis."

Achievements — things accomplished through great skill, effort, or persistence. "Her admirable performance in the competition left everyone speechless."

Ideas, plans, or solutions — when something is so well thought-out that it earns genuine intellectual respect. "That is an admirable approach to a very complicated problem."
How Strong Is the Word?

"Admirable" is a fairly strong word — not something you throw around casually. You would not describe a pleasant afternoon or a decent cup of coffee as "admirable." It is reserved for things that genuinely stand out, that go above the ordinary level, and that earn honest, deep respect.

That said, it is not the absolute peak of praise either. It sits in the range of sincere, solid, dignified approval — not breathless excitement, but real, thoughtful esteem.
A Subtle Shade: Admirable Can Imply Mild Surprise

Sometimes, "admirable" carries a quiet sense of pleasant surprise — as if the speaker did not fully expect such a high quality and is genuinely impressed by it. For example: "For someone so new to the job, her leadership skills are quite admirable." This doesn't mean she is barely good enough — it means she is impressively good, and the speaker is noting how that quality stands out even more given the context.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Knowing the differences between similar words sharpens your understanding of "admirable."

Praiseworthy is very close, but leans more toward being worthy of verbal praise specifically. "Admirable" carries a slightly deeper emotional weight — it's about inner respect and wonder, not just saying something nice.

Commendable means worthy of positive recognition. It's a bit more formal and institutional — you might find it in official reports or evaluations. "Admirable" feels more personal and heartfelt.

Laudable is a formal, literary synonym meaning highly worthy of praise. It means the same thing as "admirable" in most cases, but it is rarely used in everyday conversation.

Exemplary means so good that it can serve as a model or example for others to follow. It's slightly stronger than "admirable" and carries the added meaning of being a standard worth copying.

Remarkable means surprisingly unusual or impressive — but it lacks the moral or virtuous weight that "admirable" often carries. A strange coincidence can be remarkable, but not admirable. Admirable almost always implies that something good about character, effort, or virtue is being recognized.

Impressive focuses on the reaction — being struck by something great — but again, without the sense of moral worthiness that "admirable" carries.
Antonyms — The Opposites

The opposites of admirable are words like disgraceful (deserving shame), deplorable (extremely bad and worthy of strong condemnation), contemptible (deserving scorn), and shameful (causing or deserving shame). These give you a clear picture of the territory "admirable" occupies at the positive end of the spectrum.
Words That Naturally Go With "Admirable"

In real usage, you will most often see "admirable" paired with words like: admirable courage, admirable patience, admirable dedication, admirable restraint, admirable honesty, admirable composure, admirable qualities. As intensifiers, people say truly admirable, genuinely admirable, or thoroughly admirable.
Tone and Register

"Admirable" is slightly formal in tone. You will encounter it more in writing, speeches, journalism, and careful conversation than in casual everyday chatter. In very informal speech, people might say "awesome," "incredible," or "really impressive" instead. But "admirable" carries more gravity and dignity than those words — it signals thoughtful, earned respect rather than an excited reaction.
Example Sentences

Here are sentences that show the word in action, from simple to more nuanced:

"She showed admirable courage when she stood up for what was right."

"His dedication to helping others is truly admirable."

"What you did was admirable — very few people would have made the same sacrifice."

"The team displayed admirable discipline throughout the entire competition."

"While I disagree with his methods, his commitment to fairness is admirable."

That last sentence is particularly revealing. Notice that "admirable" can be used to recognize one specific quality in someone, even when you disapprove of other aspects of who they are. This shows the word's precision — it targets a quality, not necessarily a whole person.
The Single-Line Summary

Admirable means genuinely deserving of deep respect and sincere approval — because a quality, action, or achievement rises above the ordinary and naturally earns the honest admiration of those who witness it.
349:
Admiration is a warm, pleasant feeling you get when you see or think about someone or something that you find genuinely impressive, excellent, or worthy of praise. It combines respect and approval with a positive emotional warmth — not just a cold, calculated judgment, but a feeling that carries a kind of glow with it.

When you feel admiration, you are recognizing that something or someone has a quality — a skill, a character trait, an achievement, or a beauty — that stands clearly above the ordinary. You look at it and think: "This is remarkable. This deserves to be acknowledged."

Admiration can be directed at many different kinds of things:

People — for their courage, talent, intelligence, kindness, hard work, achievements, or moral character. You might admire a scientist who has spent her life finding cures for diseases, or a friend who stayed calm and helped others during a crisis.

Objects and places — the beauty of a painting, a building, a mountain landscape, or a piece of music. When you stand before the Taj Mahal and feel a sense of wonder at its beauty and craftsmanship, that feeling is admiration.

Qualities and actions — a selfless act, an honest decision made at great personal cost, extraordinary dedication, or brilliant creativity. Importantly, you don't have to admire a whole person — you can admire a specific quality they have or a specific thing they did.

Admiration is not just intellectual recognition. It carries genuine warmth. When you admire someone, you feel good just thinking about them. There is often a desire to appreciate them, to pay attention to them, to learn from them, or simply to acknowledge what they have done or who they are.

It can feel like a quiet sense of pleasure — the kind you feel when you watch a master musician play, read a beautifully written sentence, or witness an act of extraordinary human kindness.

Admiration exists on a scale from mild to very deep:

Mild admiration: "I noticed that she handled that difficult situation very gracefully. I admire that about her." — It is quiet and perhaps passing, but it is real.

Deep, lasting admiration: Someone who has inspired you for years — whose courage, wisdom, or genius has genuinely shaped the way you think about life. This kind of admiration is sustained, heartfelt, and sometimes life-changing.
How admiration differs from similar feelings

This is one of the most useful things to understand, because admiration is often confused with nearby emotions.

Admiration vs. envy: Envy is when you want what someone else has and feel resentful or unhappy because you do not have it. Admiration is when you genuinely appreciate what someone has, without bitterness and without necessarily wanting it for yourself. You can admire a great dancer without wishing you were a dancer. Envy shrinks you; admiration does not.

Admiration vs. respect: Respect is closely related to admiration but tends to be cooler and more formal. You respect someone when you recognize their authority, competence, or rights. Admiration includes that recognition but adds emotional warmth and a sense of being genuinely moved or impressed. You might respect a strict but fair employer, while you admire a mentor who lights a fire in you.

Admiration vs. love: Love is deep personal attachment — it is about a relationship. Admiration does not require personal closeness. You can admire a historical figure you have never met and never will. You can admire someone without loving them, and you can love someone without fully admiring them (though the two often go together beautifully).

Admiration vs. awe: Awe is what you feel when something is so grand or overwhelming that it makes you feel very small — like standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon or watching a violent thunderstorm over the ocean. Awe can be part of admiration, but admiration is warmer and more personal. Awe sometimes carries an edge of fear or smallness; admiration is purely positive.

Admiration vs. idolization: Idolization is an excessive, uncritical, and somewhat blind form of admiration — when you admire someone so intensely that you see no flaws in them, placing them on an unreachable pedestal. Healthy admiration can acknowledge that someone is imperfect while still genuinely valuing their excellent qualities. Idolization cannot.

Admiration is typically earned rather than given automatically. Things that commonly earn it:

  • Excellence — reaching a very high level in something: athletic greatness, intellectual mastery, artistic skill.
  • Virtue — showing qualities like honesty, courage, generosity, and integrity — especially when doing so is difficult or costly.
  • Persistence — working hard and never giving up, especially in the face of great obstacles or repeated failure.
  • Originality — thinking in a way no one has thought before, or creating something truly new and meaningful.
  • Selflessness — putting others before yourself, sacrificing your own comfort or advantage for someone else's benefit.

Admiration is not always spoken aloud. It can be expressed in several ways:

Verbally — telling someone directly, or telling others: "I really admire how she handled that," or "He is one of the most admirable people I've ever met."

By close attention — watching someone perform, reading everything they have written, or following their work carefully over time. Paying close, willing attention is itself a quiet form of admiration.

By imitation — trying to adopt the qualities or approach of the person you admire. If you admire someone's patience, you try to be more patient yourself. This is arguably the most meaningful form of admiration — it improves you.

By praise — publicly acknowledging someone's achievements or qualities, making sure others see what you see.

"hold someone in admiration" — to think of someone with a lasting, respectful admiration.
"I have always held her in great admiration."

"earn someone's admiration" — to do something that causes someone to admire you.
"His bravery during the rescue earned the admiration of the entire community."

"worthy of admiration" — deserving to be admired.
"Her dedication to her work is truly worthy of admiration."

"mutual admiration" — when two people admire each other.
"There was a clear mutual admiration between the two scientists."

"admiration for" — the most natural preposition used with this noun.
"She expressed her admiration for the artist's work."

"lost in admiration" — so deeply moved by admiration that you are momentarily still or speechless.
"He stood lost in admiration before the ancient sculpture."

1. "The crowd watched in silent admiration as the gymnast completed her routine without a single error."
  2. "Her admiration for her grandmother's quiet strength only grew as she learned more about what the woman had endured."
  3. "He had always felt a deep admiration for teachers who could make complicated things simple."
  4. "The novel received widespread admiration for its honesty and the beauty of its language."
  5. "It takes nothing away from your own abilities to feel admiration for someone else's talent."
  6. "His colleagues spoke of him with great admiration, praising both his skill and his personal decency."
  7. "She looked at the mountains with the kind of admiration that made her feel, for a moment, very peaceful."

Admiration is a generous emotion. It costs you nothing to feel it, and it does not diminish you in any way. When you genuinely admire someone, it reflects well on you — it shows that you are capable of recognizing greatness and goodness outside yourself.

It is also one of the emotions that can quietly guide and shape you. The things you find yourself admiring most often reveal a great deal about what you value and, perhaps, what you quietly hope to become.
